text:
First, let’s get the Pep Exception out of the way. Or perhaps we’d better call it the Guardiola Caveat. Regardless, the point is the same. If US Soccer can get Pep Guardiola to manage the United States men’s national team, it should. Because when you have the chance to employ the most successful and influential coach of his generation, the thinker who stands upstream of essentially every major tactical current of the last two decades, you just have to do it.
But let us assume that US Soccer can’t appoint Guardiola, because he is only a few months into his post-Manchester City sabbatical and still busying himself defending his body of work. Because he has given no recent indication that he wants the job, even though he spent a previous break between managerial gigs living in New York City and was probably only being supportive of his newly-appointed colleague Mauricio Pochettino when he called the project “fascinating” two years ago. Also because he has only ever signed on to coach teams stacked with Ballon d’Or contenders, posing a Phil Jackson-type, bar-room question over whether he would still be exceptional in charge of unexceptional players.
The federation has already begun its search for a successor to Pochettino. The Argentine oversaw just over two years at the head of the USMNT, a successful if hardly transformative period, but has now set off on a bold quest to cure Manchester United of their misery. “Our guide for the types of managers that we would consider is not based on the level of fame or celebrity,” the federation’s chief operating office, Dan Helfrich, told the Athletic. “But it is based on a very high standard of excellence, and ambition, and talent, and experience, and belief”. There was more such word-salad pabulum about moving “at the pace that the situation dictates”, but the long and short of it is that US Soccer is apparently willing to consider any candidate at all.
The federation expects to have the same type of billionaire donor backing that underwrote Pochettino’s $6m annual salary – which was about double that of Jürgen Klinsmann, the previous highest-earning USMNT manager. Much of it came from hedge-funder Ken Griffin, who got better value out of the last-16 World Cup performance posted by Pochettino than the $40m he set on fire supporting Republicans in the midterm election.
Helfrich is right in surmising that it makes little sense to prioritize resume over compatibility in the new man, assuming that it is a man and dismissing, with great prejudice, TNT analyst Kyle Martino’s half-cocked idea of putting Emma Hayes in charge of both senior national team programs, as if coaching the women’s team somehow isn’t a full-time job on its own.
It’s nice that the federation can afford just about anyone these days, and a stark departure from previous coaching searches. In 1991, Bora Milutinović got the gig in part because he was far cheaper than any of the other seasoned international coaches, although the Serb seems to have compensated for this by having his salary sent to some kind of offshore holding company. But at this stage of the cycle, and without a seminal World Cup looming on a home soil, nevermind a slumping core of key players to kickstart, the job is different.
Presently this isn’t a sales job in the way it was before this summer. And even if it were, it’s debatable whether having even a manager with Pochettino’s stature moved the needle in the American mainstream. Pochettino was rarely seen on any of the remaining TV shows of influence, or, but for a single hit on the Pat McAfee Show, on the podcasts that now set the agenda. He didn’t go on the late-night talk shows, the sort of thing even his affectless predecessor, Bob Bradley, managed to do. No amount of soccer coaching fame, it seems, suffices to gain traction in the today’s fractured media landscape … short of, perhaps, Guardiola’s.
Which begs the question of whether paying for Pochettino’s fame premium yielded a return off the field. Mind you, the 54-year-old was, and presumably remains, a good coach. His appointment made sense for the stage the USMNT was in. But his successor will stare down three-and-a-half years of Concacaf tournaments and World Cup qualifiers, with a Copa América in the summer of 2028. That’s a lot of trips to San Pedro Sula and Port of Spain and the Azteca.
The work of refreshing a golden generation that will be at the tail end of their primes by 2030 and integrating the latest wave of tantalizingly talented teenagers is presently more urgent than proselytizing. Right now, the program doesn’t need an exciting figurehead; it needs a competent bureaucrat who will quietly do the finnicky work of fine-tuning a team that’s trending upwards.
And so Steve Cherundolo and BJ Callaghan may not excite in the way that a name with a fun pronunciation that you recall seeing in the Premier League might, but generating buzz isn’t in the job description just now; ensuring continuity and parlaying momentum from six straight post-World Cup wins is. Better to do it with a coach who already knows the player pool and the path through all the unexciting bits of the World Cup cycle.
- Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.
digest_he:
התאחדות הכדורגל של ארצות הברית החלה בחיפוש אחר מאמן חדש שיחליף את מאאוריציו פוצ'טינו שעזב למנצ'סטר יונייטד. בכירים בהתאחדות הבהירו כי הדגש בבחירת המאמן הבא לא יינתן על רמת הפרסום או הסלבריטאיות שלו, אלא על סטנדרטים גבוהים של מצוינות, אמביציה וניסיון מתאים לשלב הנוכחי של הנבחרת.

בעוד ששמו של פפ גוארדיולה הוזכר כמועמד אידיאלי תיאורטי, ההערכה היא כי הנבחרת זקוקה פחות לדמות מוכרת ויקרה, ויותר למאמן עבודה שיבצע את ההתאמות הדרושות וישמור על יציבות לאורך מחזור המונדיאל הקרוב. בתמיכת משקיעים מיליארדרים, ההתאחדות יכולהרשות לעצמה מגוון רחב של מועמדים, אך המטרה המרכזית נותרה שילוב דור העתיד והמשך המומנטום החיובי של הנבחרת.
